title: Watch, or Operate
subtitle: One thyroid nodule, from the first blood test to the final report
description: Interpreting a thyroid panel, choosing a needle for a deeply placed nodule, deciding when follow-up should end, preoperative documentation and imaging, risk stratification, and the decision that follows surgery.

steps.title: Step 1/7: Reading the Panel
steps.scenario:
A 44-year-old woman is referred to your clinic with a right thyroid nodule found on a neck ultrasound. She has no compressive symptoms, no voice change, no radiation history and no family history of thyroid cancer.

Her thyroid panel (institutional reference range in brackets):

    TSH                     1.76 uIU/mL      [0.34 - 5.60]
    Free T4                 0.98 ng/dL       [0.61 - 1.44]
    T3                      105 ng/dL        [87 - 178]
    Anti-TPO antibody       40.2 IU/mL   (H) [< 34]
    Thyroglobulin           > 300 ng/mL  (H) [1.4 - 78]
    Anti-thyroglobulin      1.8 IU/mL        [< 4]
    TSH receptor antibody   0.8 IU/L         [< 1.75]
steps.question: How do you read this panel?

options.text: (A) A thyroglobulin above 300 ng/mL indicates a high tumor burden and argues for prompt surgery
(B) The raised anti-TPO points to thyroiditis and makes malignancy less likely
(C) The normal TSH means the nodule is not autonomously functioning; nothing else here changes the plan
(D) The normal anti-thyroglobulin antibody means the thyroglobulin can be trusted as a tumor marker

steps.feedback:
Correct answer: C

TSH is the only test here that changes the pathway. If suppressed, it suggests an autonomously functioning nodule, rarely malignant, and leads to scintigraphy rather than a needle. If normal, as here, and the decision depends on ultrasound and cytology. Free T4 and T3 grade dysfunction only once TSH is abnormal; the TSH receptor antibody matters only if TSH is suppressed.

Nothing on this panel diagnoses cancer. Only calcitonin can, for medullary carcinoma, and it was not ordered.

Why the others fail:
(A) Thyroglobulin is produced by all follicular thyroid tissue, so it is not specific to malignancy.
• Its level reflects gland volume, thyroiditis, and even mechanical disruption from palpation or biopsy.
• While the thyroid gland is still in place, no single Tg threshold reliably distinguishes benign from malignant disease; the overlap between the two is substantial.
• Current ATA guidelines do not recommend routine preoperative Tg or TgAb testing for diagnostic purposes.
• Tg becomes clinically actionable only once the gland and all Tg-producing tissue has been removed.
• A preoperative Tg is therefore drawn to establish an individual baseline, not to diagnose or stage disease.
• After thyroidectomy, serial Tg measurements and their trend over time, read against that baseline and against TSH stimulation status, are used to predict persistent, recurrent, or metastatic differentiated thyroid cancer.
(B) Anti-TPO establishes thyroiditis and predicts hypothyroidism after lobectomy, but does not lower the risk of a discrete suspicious nodule.
(D) Anti-Tg tells you whether the thyroglobulin can be believed, since it falsely lowers Tg in standard assays. A true value is still not a tumor marker.

Keypoint: the TSH tells you which pathway to follow, the antibodies tell you about the gland, and the thyroglobulin tells you nothing until the thyroid is removed.

Reference: Haugen BR, Alexander EK, Bible KC, et al. Thyroid. 2016;26(1):1-133. doi:10.1089/thy.2015.0020. Giovanella L, D'Aurizio F, Petranovic Ovcaricek P, Gorges R. Diagnostic, theranostic and prognostic value of thyroglobulin in thyroid cancer. J Clin Med. 2024;13(9):2463. doi:10.3390/jcm13092463.

steps.title: Step 2/7: Long Enough to Reach
steps.scenario:
You scan her yourself. The right lobe contains a 0.51 x 0.63 x 0.58 cm nodule: solid, markedly hypoechoic, ill-defined with an irregular boundary and an incomplete halo.

It sits against the posterior border of the lobe, deep to the bulk of the gland.

You aspirate it under your own ultrasound guidance.
steps.media:
Load image 1: Transverse ultrasound of the right lobe showing the nodule at the posterior border. Caption: 'Right lobe, transverse.'
Load image 2: A 22 gauge and a 25 gauge needle side by side against a ruler. Caption: 'Needle gauges.'
steps.question: Which needle do you use?

options.text: (A) 25 to 27 gauge
(B) 22 to 23 gauge
(C) 18 gauge core needle
(D) 20 gauge with continuous strong suction

steps.feedback:
Correct answer: B

The needle has to do two things at once. It has to be thin, because blood in the sample is the main reason an aspirate comes back non-diagnostic. It also has to be long enough to reach a nodule sitting at the back of the lobe. The thinnest needles are also the shortest ones, so 22 to 23 gauge is the compromise.

Why the others fail:
(A) This is the right choice for a nodule near the surface. This one is too deep, and a needle that does not reach the target brings back normal thyroid tissue instead.
(C) A core needle is used when repeated fine needle samples are non-diagnostic, or when lymphoma is suspected. Neither applies here.
(D) Blood in the sample comes mostly from suction and from bleeding, not from the size of the needle. Strong continuous suction is the quickest way to spoil the specimen.

Keypoint: choose the needle by how deep the nodule is, not by how suspicious it looks.

Reference: Haugen BR, Alexander EK, Bible KC, et al. Thyroid. 2016;26(1):1-133. doi:10.1089/thy.2015.0020.

steps.title: Step 3/7: Six Months Later
steps.scenario:
The cytology returns papillary thyroid carcinoma.

The nodule measures 0.51 x 0.63 x 0.58 cm. Below 1 cm it is size-eligible for active surveillance, and after discussion she chooses it.

Six months later:

    Baseline     0.51 x 0.63 x 0.58 cm
    6 months     0.81 x 0.83 x 0.90 cm

On the follow-up scan the lesion now abuts the posterior thyroid capsule.
steps.media: Load image: Side-by-side ultrasound, baseline and six-month study, matched plane and scale. Caption: 'Baseline and six months.'
steps.question: Which finding ends active surveillance?

options.text: (A) The maximal diameter has increased by more than 3 mm
(B) The nodule is approaching the 1 cm ceiling for surveillance
(C) The nodule grew during the very first surveillance interval
(D) Growth of more than 3 mm in one dimension and a volume increase over 50 percent, in a lesion now abutting the posterior capsule

steps.feedback:
Correct answer: D

She meets the criteria on both counts.

Growth: the Kuma definition is an increase of 3 mm or more in any axis. Her longitudinal dimension went from 0.58 to 0.90 cm, which is 3.2 mm. NCCN uses the same 3 mm threshold and adds a volume increase of 50 percent or more; her volume went from 0.098 to 0.317 mL, over 200 percent.

Location: the lesion now abuts the posterior capsule, close to the recurrent laryngeal nerve. An unfavorable location is a reason not to offer surveillance at all, and it is also why the usual concession does not apply here. Kuma allows surveillance to continue to 13 mm only if the location is not concerning. Hers is.

Why the others fail:
(A) The maximal diameter went from 0.63 to 0.90 cm, which is 2.7 mm. The 3 mm threshold is met on the longitudinal axis, not this one.
(B) 0.90 cm is close to 1 cm, but size alone is not a trigger. The triggers are growth, nodal or distant metastasis, and extrathyroidal extension.
(C) Some growth is expected. Surveillance is built around defined thresholds rather than around any change at all.

Keypoint: measure every axis, and remember that a tumor reaching the posterior capsule ends surveillance whatever the numbers say.

Reference: National Comprehensive Cancer Network. NCCN Clinical Practice Guidelines in Oncology: Thyroid Carcinoma. Version 2.2026, June 2, 2026. Miyauchi A, Ito Y, Fujishima M, et al. Long-term outcomes of active surveillance and immediate surgery for adult patients with low-risk papillary thyroid microcarcinoma: 30-year experience. Thyroid. 2023;33(7):817-825. doi:10.1089/thy.2023.0076. Tuttle RM, Fagin JA, Minkowitz G, et al. Natural history and tumor volume kinetics of papillary thyroid cancers during active surveillance. JAMA Otolaryngol Head Neck Surg. 2017;143(10):1015-1020.

steps.title: Step 4/7: Before Surgery
steps.scenario: She agrees to a right thyroidectomy with isthmusectomy. She has no voice complaint and no prior neck surgery. You plan to use intraoperative nerve monitoring.
steps.question: What must be documented before she goes to surgery?

options.text: (A) Vocal fold mobility on laryngoscopy, and a baseline thyroglobulin with anti-thyroglobulin antibody
(B) Vocal fold mobility only; a thyroglobulin in an intact gland has no use at any stage
(C) A baseline calcium and parathyroid hormone, since hypoparathyroidism is the main risk of the procedure
(D) Nothing further; she has no voice complaint, and nerve monitoring will identify the nerve intraoperatively

steps.feedback:
Correct answer: A

Laryngoscopy is done to record the preoperative baseline of vocal fold mobility. A normal voice does not mean both folds move normally. If a fold is found to be immobile after the operation and there is no record from before, it cannot be determined whether the surgery caused it. The 2025 guidelines also support intraoperative nerve monitoring to improve voice outcomes.

On the thyroglobulin: she has been under active surveillance, and the 2025 guidelines recommend measuring Tg and TgAb during surveillance, so she already has a series on file. Drawing it once more before surgery gives a clean starting value. After a lobectomy the guidelines recommend a single Tg measurement to make sure it is not unexpectedly high, and advise against serial trending, because the remaining lobe keeps producing it. The antibody matters because a positive TgAb makes any Tg value uninterpretable.

Why the others fail:
(B) Right that Tg cannot diagnose or stage; wrong that it has no use at any stage. It is measured during surveillance and once after lobectomy.
(C) Hypoparathyroidism is uncommon when only one lobe is removed, and a baseline calcium would not change the operation.
(D) Nerve monitoring helps find the nerve during the operation and gives information about it at the end. It cannot tell you what the vocal fold was doing beforehand.

Keypoint: record the vocal folds before the operation, and know what the thyroglobulin is for at each stage.

Reference: Ringel MD, Sosa JA, Baloch Z, et al. Thyroid. 2025;35(8):841-985. Praw SS, Gigliotti BJ, Tessnow A, Kang H, Margulies DJ. Executive summary of the 2025 American Thyroid Association management guidelines for adult patients with differentiated thyroid cancer. Thyroid. 2025;35(11):1214-1220. doi:10.1177/10507256251390877. Giovanella L, D'Aurizio F, Petranovic Ovcaricek P, Gorges R. J Clin Med. 2024;13(9):2463. doi:10.3390/jcm13092463.

steps.title: Step 5/7: Which Imaging
steps.scenario: The lesion abuts the posterior thyroid capsule, which raises the question of extrathyroidal extension. Her ultrasound shows no abnormal cervical nodes.
steps.media: Load image: Contrast-enhanced CT of the neck at the level of the thyroid, unannotated. Caption: 'Axial, post-contrast.'
steps.question: What imaging do you obtain before the operation?

options.text: (A) Non-contrast CT, to avoid an iodine load before possible radioiodine
(B) No cross-sectional imaging; the ultrasound already covers the neck
(C) Contrast-enhanced CT of the neck and mediastinum
(D) Repeat ultrasound of the lateral compartments, since ultrasound is the most sensitive test for cervical nodes

steps.feedback:
Correct answer: C

The 2025 ATA guidelines recommend CT or MRI of the neck and mediastinum with intravenous contrast when there is bulky lymph node involvement or suspicion that the aerodigestive tract or mediastinum is involved (R8). Her lesion abuts the posterior capsule, which places it against the tracheoesophageal groove, and that is the suspicion the scan is there to settle. PET/CT is not recommended routinely.

Why the others fail:
(A) Without contrast the scan cannot show whether the tumor is wrapped around vessels, or whether lymph nodes are enhancing or necrotic, and those are the findings that change the operation. The iodine clears in 4 to 6 weeks, and the ATA position is that better images are worth a short delay to radioiodine. A urine iodine level can be checked if there is doubt.
(B) Ultrasound cannot see the retropharyngeal, parapharyngeal, infraclavicular or mediastinal areas, and it cannot show how far the disease extends downward.
(D) Ultrasound is very good for the lateral neck, which is how she was staged N0. The problem is the areas it cannot reach.

Keypoint: contrast is necessary here, because the findings that would change the operation cannot be seen without it.

Reference: Ringel MD, Sosa JA, Baloch Z, et al. Thyroid. 2025;35(8):841-985, Recommendation 8. Praw SS, Gigliotti BJ, Tessnow A, Kang H, Margulies DJ. Executive summary of the 2025 American Thyroid Association management guidelines for adult patients with differentiated thyroid cancer. Thyroid. 2025;35(11):1214-1220. doi:10.1177/10507256251390877.

steps.title: Step 6/7: Reading the Report
steps.scenario:
Final pathology:

    Papillary thyroid carcinoma, tall cell subtype, well differentiated
    Two foci, right lobe: 1.1 cm and 0.3 cm
    Extrathyroidal extension: not identified
    Vascular and lymphatic invasion: not identified
    Margin: tumor close to peripheral margin, less than 0.1 mm
    Lymph nodes: perithyroid 0/1, level VI 0/2
    pT1b(m) pN0
steps.media: Load image: Final pathology report, all patient and institutional identifiers redacted. Caption: 'Final histology.'
steps.question: Where does she fall in the 2025 ATA recurrence risk stratification?

options.text: (A) Low risk, because the tumor is under 2 cm and node-negative
(B) Intermediate-high risk, because of the tall cell subtype
(C) Low-intermediate risk, because of unilateral multifocality
(D) High risk, because the margin is under 0.1 mm

steps.feedback:
Correct answer: B

The 2025 ATA guidelines divide structural recurrence risk into four groups: low (under 10 percent), low-intermediate (10 to 15 percent), intermediate-high (16 to 30 percent), and high (over 30 percent).

Aggressive histology on its own moves a T1 or T2 tumor into the intermediate-high group, and tall cell is one of the listed aggressive subtypes. She also has unilateral multifocality, which by itself would only reach low-intermediate, but the histology decides the category.

Why the others fail:
(A) Low risk requires a unifocal T1 or T2 tumor with negative nodes and no aggressive histology. She fails on two counts: two foci, and tall cell.
(C) Unilateral multifocality is a low-intermediate factor, and if it were her only adverse feature that is where she would sit. Tall cell overrides it.
(D) A margin that is close but has no tumor at the edge is a negative margin. In the 2025 system, even a microscopically positive margin only changes the category if it is posterior. An anterior R1 stays in the low-risk group, the same as a negative margin, because in front of the capsule there is only strap muscle, the surgical clearance there is small by nature, and recurrence at that site is uncommon and easy to manage. A posterior R1 moves to low-intermediate, because behind the gland lie the recurrent laryngeal nerve, trachea, and esophagus. Only gross residual disease (R2) reaches high risk. Her margin is negative, and less than 0.1 mm of clearance does not move her category at all.

Keypoint: aggressive histology alone takes a small node-negative tumor to intermediate-high; a close negative margin is still negative, and even a positive margin only matters if it is posterior.

Reference: Ringel MD, Sosa JA, Baloch Z, et al. 2025 American Thyroid Association Management Guidelines for Adult Patients with Differentiated Thyroid Cancer. Thyroid. 2025;35(8):841-985, Figure 2.

steps.title: Step 7/7: What Happens Now
steps.scenario: She has had a right thyroidectomy with isthmusectomy. The left lobe is still there. The pathology shows tall cell subtype and two foci. She asks what happens next.
steps.question: What is the next step?

options.text: (A) Proceed to radioiodine now
(B) Start levothyroxine and suppress TSH below 0.1
(C) Annual ultrasound alone
(D) Discuss completion thyroidectomy, because radioiodine may be needed and it cannot be given with a lobe in place

steps.feedback:
Correct answer: D

Two findings on her report make a second operation worth discussing: tall cell subtype and two separate foci. Both raise the possibility that she will need radioiodine. Radioiodine cannot be given while the left lobe remains, because the normal lobe takes up the iodine instead of any residual disease. The first decision is therefore whether to remove the left lobe, and that is a discussion with the patient rather than an automatic step.

The 2025 ATA guidelines name tall cell as a subtype for which completion thyroidectomy may be considered after lobectomy. They also add a new recommendation: confirm that the recurrent laryngeal nerve on the operated side is functioning before operating on the contralateral side (R16). This is why her preoperative laryngoscopy mattered. NCCN gives the same guidance for positive margins, lymphatic invasion, or high-grade histology.

Why the others fail:
(A) Radioiodine cannot be given yet, because the left lobe is still in place. Since 2015 radioiodine has also been used selectively rather than routinely after surgery.
(B) This is the older approach. Before 2015, TSH suppression was routine after thyroid cancer surgery. The 2025 guidelines simplify the target to two options: within the normal reference range, or below it. Below normal is reserved for patients with biochemically or structurally incomplete response. She has no evidence of disease, so the target is the normal range. Long-term suppression also increases the risk of atrial fibrillation and reduces bone density.
(C) For a low-risk tumor under 2 cm, lobectomy with ultrasound follow-up is sufficient. She is not low risk: tall cell subtype and multifocality place her in the intermediate-high group. The close margin is negative and does not change this. Ultrasound alone leaves the question of further treatment unanswered.

Keypoint: decide about the left lobe first, because radioiodine is not an option while it remains.

Reference: Ringel MD, Sosa JA, Baloch Z, et al. Thyroid. 2025;35(8):841-985. Praw SS, Gigliotti BJ, Tessnow A, Kang H, Margulies DJ. Executive summary of the 2025 American Thyroid Association management guidelines for adult patients with differentiated thyroid cancer. Thyroid. 2025;35(11):1214-1220. doi:10.1177/10507256251390877. National Comprehensive Cancer Network. NCCN Clinical Practice Guidelines in Oncology: Thyroid Carcinoma. Version 2.2026, June 2, 2026.
